content.text:
**Block `kPg_0_-lh`** is an untitled design doc for one change: *letting an MCP server talk to a space's data without ever getting the space password.* It has four parts — Proposal, Spec, Design, Tasks.

## The problem

Today every plugin (Roam, Obsidian) signs in as one shared "space account" using a **space password**.

```
        space password
             │
    ┌────────┼────────┐
    ▼        ▼        ▼
 Roam     Obsidian   MCP?   ← if you give it the password,
 plugin   plugin            it's in forever, and the only
                            way out is changing the password
                            → which logs everyone else out too
```

## The fix

The plugin logs in a **second time**, gets a fresh session, and hands *only that session's refresh token* to the MCP. The password stays put.

```
 Plugin (already signed in)
     │ opens a throwaway client
     │ (persistSession:false, autoRefresh:false)
     ▼
 New session ──► registers itself in `mcp_session` table (id + label)
     │
     └──► handoff bundle ──► MCP
          (URL, anon key, space ID, refresh token)
          shown ONCE, never stored by the plugin
```

Now that one session can be killed on its own, without touching anybody else.

## What ships when

| | v0 (now) | Right after v0 (not yet agreed) |
|---|---|---|
| Hand a session to an MCP | ✅ | |
| `mcp_session` registry table | ✅ | |
| MCP signs *itself* out | ✅ | |
| Plugin lists + signs out one MCP | | ⏳ `sign_out_mcp_session()` |
| Password-change lockdown | | ⏳ two Supabase settings |
| Restricted / read-only MCP access | ❌ separate ticket (`agent-read-only-access`) | |

So **v0 MCP = full power of the space account, and no way to revoke it** except the emergency "sign out everyone" switch. That trade-off is the one open question (task 0.4) and needs a group decision.

## The password trap (the subtlest bit)

```
MCP session ──can it change the space password?──► YES, today
                     │
                     ├─ it would lock out every plugin
                     └─ and it could re-login under the new password,
                        escaping the registry → revocation useless

Fix part 1: secure_password_change  → blocks it, but only after 24h
Fix part 2: "require current password" → closes the 24h hole
            ⚠️ can only be set on hosted Supabase, not in config.toml
               (so no local cucumber test for it)
```

## Status

- **Settled** (with Marc-Antoine Parent, Oct 31): dedicated session not password/JWT/OAuth; v0 = full permissions; sign-out by deleting the `auth.sessions` row; both password settings on; any plugin user may connect an MCP.
- **Open:** whether revocation + password settings are in v0 or right after.
- **Tickets:** none yet — every task says "no ticket". Groups 1–4 are v0 (DB table, shared helper, Roam + Obsidian command, MCP docs); group 5 is the post-v0 batch (~1.25 days per app).

Known limits it accepts: a revoked MCP keeps its access token for up to 1 hour; the bundle is a bearer secret; the MCP must run as a single instance or refresh-token rotation may kill the session.

I'm still unclear on how the handoff bundle is used by the MCP client to log in. So walk me through the flow where a user sign in, let's say Claude, and they want to add our MCP via our plugin, like either via Roam or Obsidian. How would that flow work from the UX perspective, and then what happened at each of the steps?

The thing that was probably tripping you up: **the MCP never "logs in" at all.** It has no email and no password. It starts life holding a refresh token — a credential that can only do one thing: trade itself for an access token. That's the whole trick.

Here's the end-to-end, with Claude Desktop as the MCP client.

---

## Step 0 — Starting state

```
Roam plugin (or Obsidian)
  ├─ knows: space password        (block props / plugin settings)
  └─ holds: session A  ─────────► space account
                                  roam-42-anon@database.discoursegraphs.com
```

Everyone in the space signs in as this one shared account. Session A is the plugin's own, stored in localStorage under `sb-<key>-auth-token`.

---

## Step 1 — User runs "Connect MCP"

**UX:** command palette → *Discourse Graphs: Connect MCP* → a dialog asks for a label: `"Claude on my laptop"` → Connect.

**Underneath:** a *second* Supabase client is created — deliberately crippled:

```js
createClient(url, anonKey, {
  auth: { persistSession: false, autoRefreshToken: false }
})
```

| flag | why |
|---|---|
| `persistSession: false` | otherwise it writes to the same localStorage key and **clobbers the plugin's session A** |
| `autoRefreshToken: false` | otherwise it rotates the refresh token in the background and the copy you handed out is already dead |

That client calls `signInWithPassword(spaceEmail, spacePassword)` → **session B** is born. Same account, separate row in `auth.sessions`.

---

## Step 2 — Session B registers itself

Still before the user sees anything:

```
session B ──► rpc("register_mcp_session", { label: "Claude on my laptop" })
                      │
                      │  SECURITY DEFINER function reads
                      │  auth.jwt()->>'session_id'  and  'sub'
                      ▼
              INSERT INTO mcp_session (session_id, account_id, label, created)
```

The session ID is taken **from the caller's own token**, never from an argument. So nobody can register the plugin's session A and later get it killed as if it were an MCP.

---

## Step 3 — The bundle is shown, once

**UX:** a panel appears with a copy button and a warning that it won't be shown again.

```
┌─ Connect your MCP ──────────────────────────┐
│  supabaseUrl:   https://xxxx.supabase.co    │
│  anonKey:       eyJhbGciOi...   (public)    │
│  spaceId:       42                          │
│  refreshToken:  v1.M2Rk...      ← SECRET    │
│                          [ Copy ]           │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The plugin then **throws the client away without signing out** — if it signed out, it would delete session B, the very thing it just handed over. It stores nothing. Session A is untouched; the plugin is still signed in.

Three of the four fields are public config. The refresh token is the only secret, and it's a bearer secret: whoever holds it *is* the space account.

---

## Step 4 — User pastes it into Claude

**UX:** paste into the MCP server's config — Claude Desktop's `claude_desktop_config.json`, env vars, wherever that server keeps config. Restart Claude.

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "discourse-graph": {
    "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@discourse-graphs/mcp"],
    "env": { "DG_SUPABASE_URL": "...", "DG_ANON_KEY": "...",
             "DG_SPACE_ID": "42", "DG_REFRESH_TOKEN": "v1.M2Rk..." } }}}
```

⚠️ The doc doesn't actually specify the bundle's shape or paste target — that's task 4.1, still TODO, and building the MCP server is an explicit non-goal of this doc. The JSON above is my illustration, not a spec.

---

## Step 5 — The MCP "logs in" (it doesn't)

```
MCP boot
  │
  ├─ createClient(url, anonKey)
  ├─ setSession({ refresh_token })   or  refreshSession({ refresh_token })
  │        │
  │        ▼   POST /auth/v1/token?grant_type=refresh_token
  │     Supabase returns:  access_token (JWT, 1h)  +  a NEW refresh_token
  │
  └─ ✱ MUST write the new refresh token to disk ✱
```

That last line is the failure mode worth remembering. **Rotation is on**: every refresh burns the old token and issues a new one. An MCP that keeps re-reading the original token from its config works exactly once. After the 10-second reuse interval, Supabase sees the reuse as a stolen-token signal and may kill the session.

Same reason the doc says run **one instance per bundle** — two copies racing to refresh look identical to token theft.

From here every query carries the access token, which carries `session_id` in its claims — and that's what ties it back to the `mcp_session` row.

---

## Step 6 — Disconnecting

```
MCP side (in v0):
  signOut({ scope: 'local' })  ──► deletes session B's auth.sessions row
                               ──► ON DELETE CASCADE wipes mcp_session row
                               ──► plugin's session A untouched ✅

Plugin side (NOT in v0 — group 5):
  settings list ──► [Sign out] ──► sign_out_mcp_session(session_id)
```

So in **v0 only the MCP can end itself.** If Claude goes rogue or the laptop is lost, the user's only lever is the emergency `signOut({ scope: 'others' })`, which logs out every plugin instance in the space too. That's the gap task 0.4 is asking the team to accept or close.

---

## The whole thing in one picture

```
  ┌──────────┐  1. "Connect MCP" + label
  │  User    │─────────────────────────────┐
  └──────────┘                             ▼
       ▲                        ┌─────────────────────┐
       │ 3. bundle (once)       │   Roam / Obsidian   │
       │                        │   session A ────────┼──► Supabase
       │                        └──────────┬──────────┘    (space account)
       │                                   │ 2. 2nd client, no persist
       │                                   │    signIn → session B
       │                                   │    register_mcp_session(label)
       └───────────────────────────────────┘
       │ 4. paste
       ▼
  ┌──────────────┐  5. refresh_token ──► access_token (1h) ──► reads/writes
  │ Claude + MCP │     (store every rotated token!)
  └──────────────┘  6. signOut local ──► session B gone, A fine
```

The one-sentence version: **the plugin spends the password once, on the user's behalf, to mint a session it immediately gives away and forgets.**
So one space account can have multiple sessions. What are sessions in this Supabase context?

content.text:
A Supabase "session" is **one login event, stored as a row in the database.** Not a user, not a device, not a connection — a row.

```
auth.users                       auth.sessions
┌────────────────────────┐      ┌──────────┬──────────┬────────────┐
│ id:    7f3a-…          │◄─────│ id  (A)  │ user_id  │ created_at │
│ email: roam-42-anon@…  │◄─────│ id  (B)  │ user_id  │ created_at │
│ encrypted_password     │◄─────│ id  (C)  │ user_id  │ created_at │
└────────────────────────┘      └──────────┴──────────┴────────────┘
   ONE identity                   MANY sessions
```

Every call to `signInWithPassword` inserts a new row. Nothing about signing in replaces or invalidates the previous ones — which is why Trang's Roam, a teammate's Obsidian, and the handed-over MCP session all coexist under the same space account. It's the "logged-in devices" list in Gmail, except the account happens to be shared.

## A session owns two very different tokens

```
                 ┌─ access token (JWT) ──────────────────────────┐
  session B ─────┤   • ~1 KB of signed JSON, 1 hour (jwt_expiry) │
                 │   • carries: sub = user id                    │
                 │              session_id = B   ← the link back │
                 │   • verified by MATH, not a DB lookup         │
                 │   • ⇒ CANNOT be revoked. Only expires.        │
                 └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                 ┌─ refresh token ───────────────────────────────┐
                 │   • opaque string, lives in the DB            │
                 │   • only power: trade itself for a new pair   │
                 │   • rotates on every use                      │
                 │   • ⇒ CAN be revoked: delete the session row  │
                 └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

This split is the whole reason the design works the way it does. The access token is stateless, so Postgres checks the signature and reads `session_id` straight out of the claims without touching a table — that's how `register_mcp_session()` can trust `auth.jwt()->>'session_id'` as the caller's true identity. And it's also why revocation is never instant: killing a session stops *future* refreshes, but an access token already in flight stays valid for up to an hour. Hence the accepted risk in the doc.

## The lifecycle, and the one surprising bit

```
signIn ──► INSERT auth.sessions (created_at = now)
              │
              ├─ refresh ──► rotate refresh token, issue new JWT
              ├─ refresh ──► rotate again…           ⚠ row UNCHANGED,
              ├─ refresh ──► …forever                  created_at NEVER resets
              │
              └─ DELETE row ──► refresh fails; session gone
```

A refresh does **not** create a new session. That's what makes `secure_password_change` actually bite: its 24-hour clock runs off `session.created_at`, so for a handed-over MCP the countdown starts at handoff and can never be reset by staying active. 24 hours later, that session is permanently barred from changing the password.

## Current settings in `packages/database/supabase/config.toml`

| | value | consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `jwt_expiry` | `3600` | revocation lag of up to 1 hour |
| `enable_refresh_token_rotation` | `true` | each refresh token is single-use |
| `refresh_token_reuse_interval` | `10` | reuse after 10 s looks like theft → session may be killed |
| `[auth.sessions] timebox` | commented out | **sessions never expire on their own** |
| `inactivity_timeout` | commented out | idle sessions live forever too |
| `secure_password_change` | `false` | any session can change the password today |

The two commented-out lines are why a handed-over session is effectively permanent until someone deletes its row — and therefore why the registry table has to exist at all.

## Sign-out is just row deletion, scoped three ways

```
local   → DELETE my row                  MCP disconnecting itself   ✅ v0
others  → DELETE every row EXCEPT mine   the emergency switch (nukes every plugin)
global  → DELETE all rows
                 ▲
sign_out_mcp_session(id) → DELETE one specific row, but only if it's
                           registered in mcp_session for my account   ⏳ group 5
```

`auth.sessions` by itself can't tell you *which* rows are MCPs — a session ID appears nowhere except inside its own tokens. That's the entire justification for shipping `mcp_session` in v0 even if sign-out is postponed: an unregistered session can never be identified again, so registration has to start before revocation exists.
for this, does it mean that Claude and MCP has to get a new token every hour or like whenever the token expires?

Yes — every hour, for as long as it's connected. But it's automatic, and the user never sees it.

```
t=0:00  refresh ──► access token #1  ─┐
                                      │ all queries carry #1
t≈0:55  refresh ──► access token #2  ─┘  ← client does this on its own
t≈1:55  refresh ──► access token #3
        …forever, until the session row is deleted
```

`supabase-js` handles this for you: it keeps a timer and swaps the token shortly before expiry, so a query never fires with a dead one. The MCP just makes calls; the refresh happens underneath.

## The catch: every refresh also replaces the *refresh* token

```
POST /token?grant_type=refresh_token
  send: refresh_token  R1
  get:  access_token  A2   (1 hour)
        refresh_token R2   ← R1 is now DEAD
```

So the string sitting in the user's config file is only good for the **first** refresh. After that it's garbage. This is the thing that will bite whoever builds the MCP server:

```
❌  read DG_REFRESH_TOKEN from env on every boot
       → works once; every restart after that fails to authenticate

✅  read env token ONLY on first run
    then write each rotated token to a state file
    boot → load from state file → refresh → overwrite state file
```

MCP servers are usually short-lived processes — Claude Desktop starts them on launch and kills them on quit — so "boot" happens constantly. Token persistence isn't optional, it's the difference between a connector that works and one that works for an hour.

## Two clients, opposite settings

Worth separating these, because they look contradictory:

| | plugin's handoff client | MCP's own client |
|---|---|---|
| `persistSession` | `false` — must not clobber the plugin's stored session | `true` — must survive restarts |
| `autoRefreshToken` | `false` — must not rotate the token before handing it over | `true` — wants the hourly swap |

The `false, false` pair in the design doc applies *only* to the throwaway client inside the plugin, during the few seconds the bundle is being minted. The MCP wants the normal behaviour.

## What this means for revocation

```
sign out the session ──► next refresh gets 401, MCP is dead
                   but the access token it grabbed 5 minutes ago
                   ──► still works for ~55 more minutes
```

That's the up-to-an-hour lag in the doc's risk list. Shortening `jwt_expiry` would narrow it, but it applies to every user of the project, not just MCPs — so it's listed as a lever, not a plan.

One more consequence of hourly refreshes: they're the mechanism that makes "run a single instance per bundle" matter. Two copies of the MCP alive at once will both hit that hourly refresh with the same token, land outside the 10-second reuse interval, and Supabase reads that as a stolen token — potentially killing the session for both.
